doc.title: Ray Shiner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 1998

title: How Shiner got the Sauter-Finegan audition
summary: Eddie Irwin recommended him; he flubbed Moonlight on the Ganges but the band wanted him; band formed 1952.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Well listen, how did your name come up when they started to put the Sauter-Finegan band together?

They were auditioning musicians in New York when they started the band, and they said, “Does anybody know of any oboe doublers?” And this one trombone player said, “Yeah I know a guy up in Rochester.” Eddie Irwin, Eddie played in the New York Philharmonic. He says, “This guy doubles, he’s a good doubler.” He says, “I don’t call him a doubler, he plays good oboe.” So I didn’t know it was through Ed that I got the audition until I got to the rehearsal, to the audition itself, which was a combination audition-rehearsal, and I saw Ed in the trombone section and Jim Buffington, a French horn player was there. Everybody in town knew I was coming to town to audition, so they all showed up at the audition.
What did the audition consist of? Just playing some of their charts?

Just sitting in and playing the charts. And one number they played was “Moonlight on the Ganges,” and I missed every note. I was so nervous, it was so difficult. And then six months later, after I been on the band, I never figured out how I got on the band, I says to Finegan, “How come you picked me to play oboe in the band?” I says, “I missed every note on ‘Ganges.’” He said, “You played two good bars on ‘When Hearts Are Young.’” And he says, “And the guys in the band wanted you.” So, which was another thing — that was a very unusual band. We were all, it was like a family. Two players in the band said, “We want Shiner.” That was it.
It’s nice to have that support, yeah. Was there any talk about, was this a good idea to be trying to be forming a big band now, was it what, ‘52?
Yeah, ‘52. ‘53 was the first year we went on the road. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
